Verdict: ACCEPTI accept the new missing-port-to-distinct-BP-terminal injection theorem, together with the added local port-degree and adjacent-BP lemmas, under the explicitly stated freezing-certificate rule. This is a fresh assessment of the new argument.The crucial dependency set
$$U=\{D_1,\ldots,D_s\}\cup\{a_0,\ldots,a_s\}$$
is correctly chosen. Every member requires a strictly earlier freezing event within  $U$ , even when certificate events and support outside  $J$  are allowed. The proof therefore excludes the only path-component obstruction to the adjacent-terminal injection.I found no mathematical error or missing hypothesis requiring revision. The distinction between distinct BP terminals and distinct BP–BP unit-credit paths is also correct and essential. The universal compensation inequality remains unproved.I have not executed the supplied programs or Lean files, and this verdict certifies none of the reported execution results.1. The freezing hypothesis is sufficiently precise—and is doing essential workWrite  $x^\ast$  for the actual mate of an endpoint  $x$ , and let  $\tau(x)$  be its position or layer in the stated complete freezing certificate.The rule supplied in §1 says that freezing  $x$  requires two distinct neighbors
$$y,z\in N(x)\setminus\{x^\ast\},$$
each of which is either an original selection or an endpoint whose actual mate froze strictly earlier. For an endpoint witness  $y$ , the relevant condition is
$$\tau(y^\ast)<\tau(x).$$
The new proof uses this dependency direction correctly throughout. In particular, it does not substitute the freezing time of  $y$  for that of  $y^\ast$ .Because  $x^\ast$ ,  $y$ , and  $z$  are three distinct occupied original neighbors, complete freezing implies
$$\deg_{\mathrm{occ}}(x)\ge3$$
for every endpoint. This implication does not require the witness events to occur inside  $J$ .The hypotheses that matter here are already explicit:the matching used for all mate relationships is the same actual matching;witnesses are distinct and exclude the actual mate;retained endpoint witnesses require their mates to have frozen strictly earlier;all endpoints eventually freeze in a common process starting with no frozen endpoints.The argument would require a separate theorem if “complete freezing” were replaced by an unspecified exchange-terminal condition. The explicit certificate definition avoids that ambiguity. Uniqueness of the actual matching is unnecessary.2. The new exact port-degree lemma is correctThe scope of this lemma is a TP terminal of a TP–TP path, as stated in the revised note.Let  $v$  be such an endpoint, and let  $t$  be the selected other corner of its two-cell column.The actual mate is forced across the band boundarySince  $t$  already sees the occupied vertex  $v$ , feasibility makes its other neighboring vertices blank. In particular, both horizontal neighbors of  $t$  are blank.If  $v^\ast$  were horizontal, the column containing  $v^\ast$  would consequently have one endpoint and one blank corner: it would be BP. Both the original TP column and this BP column have degree one in the actual PP multigraph. Their matching edge would therefore constitute an entire TP–BP path.That contradicts the stipulated TP–TP type. The vertical neighbor of  $v$  within its own band is selected, so it cannot be the actual mate. The remaining possibility is the vertical neighbor across the band boundary. Matching closure places that mate inside  $J$ .This argument also handles a possible outer-row issue: a TP–TP terminal cannot occur where that required vertical matching neighbor does not exist.The degree formula follows exactlyThe first column is BB and the final column has a blank corner, so neither boundary column is TP. Both lateral columns therefore exist for  $v$ .The other corner of each lateral column is blank, by feasibility at  $t$ . Thus a lateral column is:BB when the corresponding horizontal neighbor of  $v$  is blank;BT when it is selected;BP when it is an endpoint.Let  $\varepsilon_L,\varepsilon_R\in\{0,1\}$  indicate whether those horizontal neighbors are occupied. The two vertical neighbors of  $v$ —its selected corner and actual mate—are fixed occupied vertices. Hence
$$\deg_{\mathrm{occ}}(v)=2+\varepsilon_L+\varepsilon_R,$$
while
$$\#\mathrm{ports}(v)=2-\varepsilon_L-\varepsilon_R.$$
Therefore
$$\boxed{\#\mathrm{ports}(v)=4-\deg_{\mathrm{occ}}(v).}$$
No freezing assumption is used.It follows that a terminal of the stipulated type is missing-port exactly when its occupied degree is four. If  $m$  counts TP–TP paths with at least one missing terminal and  $q_4$  counts their missing terminals, then
$$m\le q_4\le2m.$$
Distinct actual paths have distinct terminals, so this count has no multiplicity defect.The statement about  $u$  is correctly qualified: connecting every attachable path gives  $u=m$ . Under an arbitrary partial connector selection,  $u$  can also contain deliberately omitted attachable paths.The scope restriction to TP–TP terminals should remain explicit in future citations of this lemma. An arbitrary TP terminal can have a horizontal mate.3. The adjacent-BP lemma is correct under the degree-three hypothesisLet  $v$  be a missing TP–TP terminal. The degree formula gives occupied degree four, so both horizontal neighbors are occupied.Suppose both horizontal neighbors were selections. Each already sees  $v$ , and feasibility therefore forces the vertex immediately beside  $v^\ast$  on the corresponding side to be blank. Both horizontal neighbors of  $v^\ast$  would be blank.The mate  $v^\ast$  would then have at most its two vertical neighbors occupied:
$$\deg_{\mathrm{occ}}(v^\ast)\le2.$$
This contradicts the assumption that every endpoint has occupied degree at least three.Thus  $v$  has at least one horizontal endpoint neighbor. Its column’s other corner is blank, so that neighbor is a BP terminal.This proof establishes exactly the claimed local conclusion:each missing terminal has one or two adjacent BP endpoints;degree at least three alone does not establish a simultaneous distinct assignment.The new theorem supplies the additional ownership step using the full freezing certificate.4. The horizontal incidence graph has precisely the claimed geometryThe sets  $A$  and  $D$  are disjoint: an endpoint belongs to one column of the packet, whose type cannot simultaneously be TP and BP.Every  $A$ -vertex has degree one or two in  $H$ , by the adjacent-BP lemma. Every  $D$ -vertex has degree at most two because only its two horizontal neighboring positions can supply edges of  $H$ .More importantly, an edge of  $H$  is an ordinary horizontal grid edge. Each connected component lies in one physical row, hence in one band, and is a subgraph of a finite line. This proves acyclicity directly. The argument is stronger than merely observing maximum degree two, which by itself would allow cycles.There are no isolated vertices:an  $A$ -vertex has an adjacent BP endpoint;a  $D$ -vertex is included only because it is adjacent to an  $A$ -vertex.Every component is therefore a nontrivial alternating path.The componentwise matching classification is correct:opposite endpoint types give equal numbers of  $A$  and  $D$ ;two  $D$ -ends give one extra  $D$ ;two  $A$ -ends give one extra  $A$ , making saturation of  $A$  impossible.Thus excluding an  $A$ – $A$  component is sufficient. There is no additional Hall obstruction hidden in this graph class.5. The closed-dependency proof excludes an  $A$ – $A$  componentThis is the central new argument, and its geometric implications check out.Suppose a component has vertices
$$A_0,D_1,A_1,\ldots,D_s,A_s,\qquad s\ge1.$$
Because it is connected along a row, these are consecutive positions. After choosing the vertical orientation as in the note, write
$$\begin{aligned}
A_i&=(r,c+2i),\\
D_j&=(r,c+2j-1).
\end{aligned}$$
All the  $A_i$  lie in the same row of the same band, so their selected intraband neighbors are consistently in row  $r-1$ .All the required mates have the asserted positionsThe local lemma gives
$$a_i=A_i^\ast=(r+1,c+2i).$$
For  $D_j$ , the neighbor in row  $r-1$  is blank because its column is BP. Its two horizontal neighbors are  $A_{j-1}$  and  $A_j$ , both already matched to their vertical mates  $a_{j-1},a_j$ . Neither can be the actual mate of  $D_j$ .The only possible matching neighbor is consequently
$$d_j=D_j^\ast=(r+1,c+2j-1).$$
These are distinct original endpoints at distinct positions. No matching-uniqueness assumption has been used.The outer horizontal sites beside  $a_0,a_s$  are blankConsider the horizontal neighbor of  $A_0$  outside the displayed segment. It exists because TP columns are internal, and it is occupied because  $A_0$  has no port.If it were an endpoint, its column would be BP and its adjacency to  $A_0$  would be an edge of  $H$ . The component would extend past  $A_0$ , contradicting that  $A_0$  is an endpoint of the component.It is therefore selected. It already sees  $A_0$ , so feasibility forces the vertex immediately below it to be blank. That vertex is exactly the outer horizontal neighbor of  $a_0$ .The same argument applies at  $A_s,a_s$ . This is the necessary end condition: neither end mate acquires a second unconstrained horizontal support.Each  $D_j$  requires earlier members of  $U$ Define
$$U=\{D_1,\ldots,D_s\}\cup\{a_0,\ldots,a_s\}.$$
The only nonmate occupied neighbors of  $D_j$  are
$$A_{j-1},A_j.$$
Its upper neighbor is blank and its lower neighbor  $d_j$  is its excluded actual mate.Both  $A$ -neighbors must therefore be usable endpoint witnesses when  $D_j$  freezes. Under the stated rule this requires
$$\tau(a_{j-1})<\tau(D_j),
\qquad
\tau(a_j)<\tau(D_j).$$
Both predecessors belong to  $U$ .Each  $a_i$  requires an earlier  $D_j$ The actual mate  $A_i$  lies above  $a_i$  and is excluded as a witness.The horizontal neighboring endpoints inside the segment are: $d_1$  for  $a_0$ ; $d_i,d_{i+1}$  for an interior  $a_i$ ; $d_s$  for  $a_s$ .The other horizontal site at an end is blank, as proved above. Apart from these sites, the only remaining nonmate position is the single vertex in row  $r+2$ .Consequently, two distinct witnesses for  $a_i$  must include at least one horizontal  $d_j$ . Since  $d_j$  is an endpoint, using it requires
$$\tau(d_j^\ast)=\tau(D_j)<\tau(a_i).$$
Again the necessary predecessor belongs to  $U$ .The earliest-event contradiction is validThe set  $U$  is nonempty and finite. Complete freezing gives every member a finite certificate rank. Choose a member of minimum rank.If it is a  $D_j$ , an  $a_i\in U$  must have frozen earlier. If it is an  $a_i$ , a  $D_j\in U$  must have frozen earlier. Either case contradicts minimality.This excludes the proposed  $A$ – $A$  component.Arbitrary exterior support does not break the proofThe proof does not require  $U$  to be spatially isolated, or require the certificate to stay inside  $J$ .The neighbor of  $a_i$  in row  $r+2$  may be selected, retained, outside  $J$ , or made available through an arbitrarily complicated exterior certificate. It still occupies only one neighboring position and can supply at most one witness.Even granting that witness before any event in  $U$ , freezing  $a_i$  still requires a horizontal  $d_j$ , and hence an earlier  $D_j\in U$ . The dependency obstruction therefore survives arbitrary exterior events consistent with the stated feasibility and certificate hypotheses.This is the precise reason the exterior cannot provide an escape. No bound on the exterior’s size or freezing depth is being assumed.6. The injection is constructive and has the stated ownership scopeEvery component of  $H$  now has a  $D$ -endpoint. Starting at such an endpoint and assigning each encountered  $A$  to the immediately preceding  $D$  matches all its  $A$ -vertices.If the other endpoint is also  $D$ , one  $D$  remains unused. Otherwise every vertex is paired. Different components have disjoint vertices, so these assignments combine into an adjacency-preserving injection
$$f:A\hookrightarrow D.$$
For  $A=\varnothing$ , the empty function supplies the trivial case.Every assigned image is a distinct actual BP endpoint. There is no virtual support, reused endpoint, or identification of two physical terminals in this construction.The numerical consequence is terminal capacity:
$$|A|\le |D|\le 2\beta+\gamma,$$
because a BP–BP path has two BP terminals and a TP–BP path has one. This does not yield a bound by  $\beta$ , or an assignment to distinct BP–BP paths.The earlier frozen missing-port family correctly demonstrates the limitation. Each block has two missing terminals and  $\beta=0$ ; its adjacent BP terminals lie on mixed TP–BP paths. Thus the new theorem can supply a nonempty adjacent-terminal injection while supplying no BP–BP unit credits at all.The proposed continuation by terminal cancellation remains a separate problem. The text correctly requires new proofs of ownership, multiplicity, and termination before using such a continuation in
$$h_2+u\le h_0+\beta.$$
7. The degree-three counterexample is exactThe  $4\times10$  example in §5 is feasible: each of its eight selections has exactly one occupied neighbor.The endpoint degrees are:EndpointsOccupied degree $(1,2),(1,4),(1,6)$  $4$  $(1,3),(1,5)$  $3$  $(2,4)$  $4$  $(2,2),(2,3),(2,5),(2,6)$  $3$ For the specified vertical matching, columns  $2,4,6$  give three TP–TP paths, while columns  $3,5$  give two BP–BP paths. Thus
$$\alpha=3,\qquad \beta=2.$$
The missing-terminal set is exactly
$$A=\{(1,2),(1,4),(1,6),(2,4)\}.$$
In the upper band, its incidence component is
$$A-D-A-D-A,$$
so at most two of those three  $A$ -vertices can be assigned. In the lower band the component is
$$D-A-D,$$
which contributes one assignment. The maximum adjacent-terminal matching therefore has size exactly
$$2+1=3<4.$$
The freezing calculation is also correct. Initially only  $(1,2)$  and  $(1,6)$  have two original selected nonmate witnesses. Freezing them makes their mates  $(2,2)$  and  $(2,6)$  available as endpoint witnesses.After those two events, every other endpoint still has fewer than two eligible nonmate witnesses. Hence this is a fixed point: exactly two endpoints freeze and eight remain unfrozen.The stated obstruction set is
$$U=\{(1,3),(1,5),(2,2),(2,4),(2,6)\}.$$
Its dependency structure is exactly the one used in the proof.Finally, the example does not violate the packet or global target:
$$|T|=8,\qquad |M|=5,\qquad
S=20-8-5=7.$$
Here  $k=t=2$ , so  $B=4$  and  $S-B=3>0$ . It refutes the weaker adjacent-injection assertion under occupied degree at least three, as claimed.8. The formal and computational scope is accurately limitedThe new Lean lemmas express the correct abstract principle: a nonempty set cannot have every member depend on another member of strictly smaller natural-number rank. The two-class version matches the  $D_j$ -to- $a_i$  and  $a_i$ -to- $D_j$  dependencies.The formal source does not itself establish:the geometric mate classification;the blank sites at the ends of an  $A$ – $A$  component;the row-path structure of  $H$ ;the extraction of certificate ranks from a particular implementation;the final grid-level injection.Those remain written arguments, and §6 says so.Likewise, the Boolean port lemmas establish the arithmetic once the two fixed occupied vertical neighbors have been identified. The written grid argument supplies that identification. The missing-terminal count lemma assumes the corresponding one-or-two-per-path inventory.The visible checker’s blocked-set test is consistent with the proof: a  $D_j$  has no witness whose availability is independent of earlier events in  $U$ , while an  $a_i$  has at most one. Its set named outside concerns dependencies outside  $U$ , not merely locations outside the packet.These source-level observations support the stated division of scope. They do not establish that the checker ran, that imported routines implement the intended certificate rule, or that Lean compilation and axiom audits completed successfully.
